ACE stands for Angiotensin Converting Enzyme. It converts Ang I to Ang IIAng II is a potent vasoconstrictor and causes receptors in the heart to increase cardiomyocyte output and cause release of aldosterone from adrenal cortex which increases blood pressure. By blocking ACE we stop production of Ang II and thus reduce blood pressure. ACE also has other functions such as breaking down opioid peptides and processing ADH into its active form but these effects are not significant enough to warrant ACE-i treatment. ACE-II is the equivalent drug for treatment of Heart failure. It blocks neprilysin which breaks down Angiotensin II to Angiotensin I. This prevents removal of Ang II and therefore raises levels. This encourages reuptake of renin and thus increases RAAS. It also blocks the breakdown of ADH so increased thirst and decreased Na+ excretion. All antihypertensive drugs have side effects. For example ACE-I can cause dry coughs and ACE-II can cause hyperkalaemia.  Source: 'Case 12 Clinical Biochemistry' lecture in PCS unit 3. 'Cardiac tamponade' is essentially a medical emergency where the compression of the heart against the great vessels and lung prevents it filling and emptying properly leading to reduced perfusion and oxygen supply.
